# Reaction networks and moment closure {#sec-reaction-networks}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 2, Session 3. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd).
:::

Every model so far has been written as *states changing*: a right-hand side for
$dS/dt$, a drift and diffusion for $(S,I,R)$, a pair of jump affects. Each time
we changed the mathematical setting we rewrote the model.

This chapter changes what we write down. Instead of the dynamics of the states,
we specify the **flows** — the transmission event and the recovery event, each
with the rate at which it fires and the change it makes. That specification is a
**reaction network**, and it is enough to generate the ODE, the SDE and the jump
process mechanically. It also unlocks something the state view cannot easily
give us: equations for the *moments* of the stochastic process, so we can
approximate the mean and variance of an ensemble without simulating it.

## Learning goals

You will:

- write the SIR model as a reaction network of flows rather than state equations;
- generate ODE, SDE and jump models from that one specification and check they
  agree with the hand-written versions of @sec-ordinary-differential-equations,
  @sec-stochastic-differential-equations and @sec-jump-processes;
- derive why the moment hierarchy of a bimolecular reaction does not close; and
- apply a normal closure and judge it against a jump-process ensemble.

## Model assumptions and classification

The population, parameters and baseline are unchanged from
@sec-jump-processes: a closed, homogeneously mixing $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$ with
$N=1000$, $c=10.0$, $\beta=0.05$, $\gamma=0.25$, and the composite rate constant
$\kappa=\beta c/N$.

What changes is the *description*, not the model. A reaction network is not a
fourth kind of model sitting alongside the ODE, SDE and jump process: it is a
specification from which each of those three is derived. Its classification is
therefore inherited from whichever lowering we choose — deterministic and
continuous for the ODE, stochastic and continuous for the SDE, stochastic and
discrete for the jump process. The moment equations introduced later are a
fourth, different object: deterministic equations describing a stochastic
process.

The one modelling assumption the network itself encodes is **mass action**: the
transmission flow is proportional to the number of $S$–$I$ pairs and the
recovery flow to the number of infectives.

## Equations

A reaction network is a set of reactions, each carrying a rate constant, the
species it consumes, and the species it produces:

$$
S + I \xrightarrow{\ \kappa\ } 2I,
\qquad
I \xrightarrow{\ \gamma\ } R.
$$ {#eq-ch06-network}

From this we read off the two objects that generate everything else. The
**stoichiometry matrix** $V$ collects the state change of each reaction as a
column, and the **propensity** $a_j(X)$ gives the rate at which reaction $j$
fires in state $X=(S,I,R)$:

$$
V = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 1 & -1\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
a(X) = \begin{pmatrix} \kappa S I\\ \gamma I \end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-ch06-stoichiometry}

These are exactly the $V$ and $a$ of @sec-stochastic-differential-equations,
which is the point: the pair $(V, a)$ *is* the model, and the three settings we
have used are three ways of turning it into dynamics.

| Lowering | Construction | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| ODE | $\dot X = V a(X)$ | @sec-ordinary-differential-equations |
| SDE | $dX = Va(X)\,dt + V\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{a(X)})\,dW$ | @sec-stochastic-differential-equations |
| Jump | event $j$ fires at rate $a_j(X)$, adding $V_{\cdot j}$ | @sec-jump-processes |

: The same $(V,a)$ generates all three models. {#tbl-ch06-lowerings}

### The chemical master equation and its moments

The jump process is the exact model, and its probability distribution
$P(x,t)=\Pr\{X(t)=x\}$ obeys the **chemical master equation**

$$
\frac{\partial P(x,t)}{\partial t}
= \sum_{j} \Big[ a_j(x - V_{\cdot j}) P(x - V_{\cdot j}, t) - a_j(x) P(x,t) \Big],
$$ {#eq-ch06-cme}

one equation for every reachable state. For a closed SIR population of $N=1000$
that is on the order of $10^{5}$ coupled equations — solvable in principle, and
the subject of the finite-state projection appendix, but not something we want
to carry around.

Rather than the whole distribution, we usually want a few summaries: the mean
number infectious, and how variable it is between outbreaks. Multiplying
@eq-ch06-cme by $x$ and summing gives an exact equation for the mean,

$$
\frac{d\,\mathbb{E}[X]}{dt} = V\,\mathbb{E}[a(X)].
$$ {#eq-ch06-mean}

Here is the crux. For recovery, $\mathbb{E}[\gamma I] = \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[I]$:
the propensity is linear, so its expectation depends only on the mean. But
transmission is **bimolecular**, and

$$
\mathbb{E}[\kappa S I] = \kappa\big(\mathbb{E}[S]\,\mathbb{E}[I] + \operatorname{Cov}(S,I)\big)
\neq \kappa\,\mathbb{E}[S]\,\mathbb{E}[I]
$$ {#eq-ch06-unclosed}

unless $S$ and $I$ are uncorrelated. So the equation for the first moments
requires the second moments. Writing equations for the second moments brings in
the third, and so on: the hierarchy never closes. This also explains something
seen in @sec-jump-processes — the mean of an ensemble is *not* the ODE solution.
The ODE is what you get by dropping $\operatorname{Cov}(S,I)$ from
@eq-ch06-unclosed, and during an epidemic that covariance is strongly negative,
which is why the ODE peak sits above the ensemble mean.

**Moment closure** cuts the hierarchy off. We keep moments up to some order $m$
and express the ones above $m$ in terms of those below, by *assuming* a
distributional shape. The **normal closure** used below sets the third central
moments to zero, which is what a multivariate normal distribution would give.
The assumption is about the shape of the distribution, not about the model, and
it is an approximation that can be good, poor, or numerically catastrophic.

## Julia implementation

`@reaction_network` takes the reactions of @eq-ch06-network almost verbatim.
This is the same network built in @sec-jump-processes, where it was used only to
drive a jump process; here it is the single source for every lowering.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-setup
using Catalyst
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using StochasticDiffEq
using JumpProcesses
using MomentClosure
using CairoMakie
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

const N = 1000
const β = 0.05
const c = 10.0
const γ = 0.25
const κ = β * c / N
const tspan = (0.0, 40.0)
const times = collect(0.0:0.5:40.0)

sir_network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I --> 2I
    γ, I --> R
end
```

The network knows its own species, parameters and stoichiometry, so $V$ of
@eq-ch06-stoichiometry need not be typed in by hand.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-structure
(species = species(sir_network),
 parameters = parameters(sir_network),
 V = netstoichmat(sir_network))
```

### Three models from one specification

Each lowering is a problem constructor applied to the same object. Initial
conditions are floating point for the continuous lowerings and integer for the
jump process, because a CTMC state counts individuals.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-lowerings
parameter_map = [:κ => κ, :γ => γ]
u₀_continuous = [:S => 990.0, :I => 10.0, :R => 0.0]
u₀_discrete   = [:S => 990,   :I => 10,   :R => 0]

ode_solution = solve(
    ODEProblem(sir_network, u₀_continuous, tspan, parameter_map),
    Tsit5(); saveat = times)

sde_solution = solve(
    SDEProblem(sir_network, u₀_continuous, tspan, parameter_map),
    LambaEM(); seed = 20250906, saveat = times)

jump_solution = solve(
    JumpProblem(sir_network, u₀_discrete, tspan, parameter_map;
                aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(20250906)),
    SSAStepper(); saveat = times)

(ode_peak  = round(maximum(ode_solution[2, :]); digits = 2),
 sde_peak  = round(maximum(sde_solution[2, :]); digits = 2),
 jump_peak = maximum(jump_solution[2, :]))
```

Nothing about the SIR model was restated to obtain these three. Changing the
network — adding an exposed class, a waning-immunity flow, a second host — would
propagate to all three automatically, which is the practical argument for
writing flows rather than states.

### Moment equations and closure

`generate_raw_moment_eqs(network, 2)` derives the exact equations for the raw
moments $\mu_{ijk} = \mathbb{E}[S^i I^j R^k]$ up to order 2. There are nine: the
three means, and the six second moments.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-moments
raw_equations = generate_raw_moment_eqs(sir_network, 2)
(equations = length(equations(raw_equations.odes)),
 order = raw_equations.m_order,
 unknowns = string.(unknowns(raw_equations.odes)))
```

These nine equations are not solvable as they stand: they refer to third-order
moments, exactly as @eq-ch06-unclosed predicted. `moment_closure` supplies the
missing relation.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-closure
#| warning: false
closed_equations = moment_closure(raw_equations, "normal")
closure_solution = solve(
    ODEProblem(closed_equations, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], tspan, parameter_map),
    Tsit5(); saveat = times)

closure_names = string.(unknowns(closed_equations.odes))
mean_index = findfirst(==("μ₀₁₀(t)"), closure_names)
second_index = findfirst(==("μ₀₂₀(t)"), closure_names)

closure_mean = closure_solution[mean_index, :]
closure_sd = sqrt.(max.(closure_solution[second_index, :] .- closure_mean .^ 2, 0.0))
(retcode = closure_solution.retcode,
 peak_mean = round(maximum(closure_mean); digits = 2))
```

`MomentClosure` still builds its `ODEProblem` through the older positional
signature, which emits a deprecation notice from ModelingToolkit; the cell above
suppresses warnings for that reason alone.

## Validation

The claim to test is that the closure reproduces what an ensemble of jump
simulations does. We run 200 independent trajectories, each with its own
deterministically chosen seed so the figure is reproducible.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-ensemble
function simulate_jump(seed)
    problem = JumpProblem(
        sir_network, u₀_discrete, tspan, parameter_map;
        aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed))
    return Array(solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = times)(times))
end

ensemble = cat((simulate_jump(6000 + k) for k in 1:200)...; dims = 3)
ensemble_mean = dropdims(mean(ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3)
ensemble_sd = dropdims(std(ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3)

@assert maximum(abs.(sum(ensemble; dims = 1) .- N)) == 0
(closure_vs_ensemble_peak_gap =
    round(maximum(closure_mean) - maximum(ensemble_mean[2, :]); digits = 2),
 ode_vs_ensemble_peak_gap =
    round(maximum(ode_solution[2, :]) - maximum(ensemble_mean[2, :]); digits = 2))
```

Population is conserved exactly in every trajectory, as the columns of $V$
require. The two gaps are the quantitative form of the argument after
@eq-ch06-unclosed: the closure tracks the ensemble mean far more closely than
the ODE does, because it retains the covariance the ODE discards.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch06-closure
#| fig-cap: "Mean and standard deviation of the infectious class from 200 jump-process trajectories (bands), the normal moment closure (solid), and the ODE (dashed). The closure recovers both the mean and the spread of the ensemble; the ODE peak sits above the ensemble mean because it discards the negative covariance between S and I."
figure = Figure(size = (760, 380))
axis = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious")

band!(axis, times,
      ensemble_mean[2, :] .- ensemble_sd[2, :],
      ensemble_mean[2, :] .+ ensemble_sd[2, :];
      color = (:grey, 0.35), label = "Ensemble mean ± sd")
lines!(axis, times, ensemble_mean[2, :]; color = :grey25, linewidth = 2,
       label = "Ensemble mean")
lines!(axis, times, closure_mean; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2,
       label = "Normal closure")
lines!(axis, times, closure_mean .+ closure_sd; color = :firebrick,
       linewidth = 1, linestyle = :dot, label = "Closure mean ± sd")
lines!(axis, times, closure_mean .- closure_sd; color = :firebrick,
       linewidth = 1, linestyle = :dot)
lines!(axis, times, ode_solution[2, :]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "ODE")
axislegend(axis; position = :rt, framevisible = false)
figure
```

A closure is an assumption, and assumptions fail. Asking for a log-normal
closure on this network produces equations the solver cannot start.

```{julia}
#| label: code-ch06-closure-failure
#| warning: false
lognormal_retcode = try
    solve(ODEProblem(moment_closure(raw_equations, "log-normal"),
                     [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], tspan, parameter_map),
          Tsit5(); saveat = times).retcode
catch error
    Symbol(typeof(error))
end
```

The failure is informative rather than embarrassing: a log-normal shape is
untenable for a compartment whose count reaches zero, and the closure inherits
that. Always check the return code, and always compare against simulation before
trusting a closure.

## Interpretation and limitations

Writing flows rather than states buys three things: one specification instead of
three, mechanical access to every lowering, and moment equations that are simply
unavailable from a hand-written right-hand side.

The costs are real. Moment closure is an *uncontrolled* approximation: unlike
reducing a timestep, there is no parameter to refine that guarantees
convergence, and the only honest check is comparison with simulation — which is
what we were trying to avoid. Closures degrade exactly where stochastic effects
matter most, when counts are small, near the start of an outbreak or near
extinction. The normal closure can also return negative variances or negative
means, both meaningless. And a closure describes the *ensemble*, not any single
outbreak: it can tell you the spread of epidemic sizes, but never the
probability that an outbreak fades out, which needs the distribution itself.

Mass action is the network's own assumption. Contact structure, households and
age mixing are not expressible as a two-reaction network, and @sec-agent-based-models
takes up the individual-level alternative.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch06-ex1}

Extend the network of @eq-ch06-network to an SEIR model by adding an exposed
class $E$, with $S + I \to E + I$ at rate $\kappa$ and $E \to I$ at rate
$\sigma = 0.5$. Starting from $(S,E,I,R)=(990,0,10,0)$, generate the ODE and
jump lowerings from the single network, and plot the ODE against the mean of 100
jump trajectories. State how the latent period changes the epidemic peak
relative to the SIR model of this chapter.

### Exercise 2 {#ch06-ex2}

For the SIR network, compare second-order normal closure against an ensemble of
200 jump trajectories at two population sizes, $N=1000$ and $N=100$, holding
$\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ fixed and scaling $\kappa=\beta c/N$ with the initial
condition $(0.99N, 0.01N, 0)$. Report the largest absolute difference between
closure mean and ensemble mean in each case, and explain the direction of the
change using the argument after @eq-ch06-unclosed.
